N: A normal heartbeat has an expected narrow QRS morphology and timing relative to neighboring beats.
A normal or bundle-branch-conducted beat follows the underlying rhythm without premature supraventricular or ventricular activation.
A normal-class beat may be sinus, left bundle branch block, right bundle branch block, atrial escape, or junctional escape.
The beat is consistent with organized physiologic activation rather than an ectopic premature ventricular complex.
Normal-class beats generally preserve a stable relationship between atrial activity and the QRS complex.
The waveform resembles the patient's recurring baseline beat morphology.
The beat does not show the characteristic wide premature morphology of a ventricular ectopic beat.
The beat is not a fusion, paced, or unclassifiable complex.
S: A supraventricular ectopic beat originates above the ventricles and usually has a relatively narrow QRS complex.
The beat occurs prematurely compared with the surrounding rhythm and may have an abnormal or hidden P wave.
Supraventricular ectopy includes atrial premature, aberrated atrial premature, junctional premature, and supraventricular premature beats.
The QRS may resemble the normal conducted beat because ventricular activation uses the usual conduction system.
An early beat with a narrow or only mildly aberrant QRS supports the supraventricular class.
The preceding RR interval is often shortened and may be followed by a noncompensatory pause.
The waveform is premature but lacks the strongly abnormal ventricular morphology typical of a PVC.
Atrial or junctional premature activation is the defining mechanism of this heartbeat class.
V: A ventricular ectopic beat originates in the ventricles and commonly produces a wide abnormal QRS complex.
A premature ventricular contraction often occurs early and is followed by a compensatory pause.
Ventricular ectopic morphology differs substantially from the patient's normal conducted beats.
The QRS complex may be broad and bizarre because ventricular activation does not follow the normal His-Purkinje pathway.
The beat may represent a premature ventricular contraction or a ventricular escape beat.
A discordant T wave may follow the abnormal ventricular depolarization.
The waveform is more consistent with ventricular origin than with a narrow supraventricular premature beat.
The beat is a ventricular complex rather than a fusion of simultaneous normal and ventricular activation.
F: A fusion beat combines simultaneous normal conducted activation and ventricular ectopic activation.
Fusion morphology is intermediate between the patient's normal QRS and ventricular ectopic QRS shapes.
The complex contains features of both a normal beat and a premature ventricular contraction.
A fusion beat may have a QRS width and contour between the normal and ventricular templates.
The beat results when sinus and ventricular impulses depolarize different portions of the ventricles.
The morphology is hybrid rather than fully normal or fully ventricular ectopic.
Comparison with neighboring normal and PVC morphologies helps identify the fusion complex.
The defining feature is mixed activation from normal conduction and a ventricular focus.
Q: The unknown class includes paced beats, fusion of paced and normal beats, and unclassifiable beats.
A paced beat may show a pacing artifact immediately before an abnormal paced QRS complex.
Fusion of paced and normal activation creates a hybrid morphology that does not fit ordinary fusion or normal classes.
An unclassifiable beat lacks sufficient reliable morphology for assignment to N, S, V, or F.
The waveform may be dominated by pacing, artifact, or an unusual morphology outside the principal AAMI groups.
This class is reserved for beats that cannot be confidently treated as normal, supraventricular, ventricular, or fusion.
A sharp pacing spike with subsequent ventricular capture supports the paced or unknown group.
Ambiguous annotation or paced activation is the defining context for the Q class.
